items.title: James Moody — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Charlie Parker was the last one I heard. That's why when I heard him, that was it.

ctx.x: When you started on alto, who were some of the people -- You like Jimmy Dorsey (phonetic sp.). I remember you said that. Were there other players beside Jimmy Dorsey and Charlie Parker who were influences on you?

Charlie Parker was the last one I heard. That's why when I heard him, that was it. That was it, yeah. But there was a guy by the name of Rudy Williams (phonetic sp.) who played with the Savoy Salton (phonetic sp.) and he was from Newark. There was, I mean, there was like Tab Smith (phonetic sp.) with Count Bassie, but I, you know, like I kind of narrowed it down because all these guys they play nice saxophone, but that wasn't the way I wanted to play. Like Bill Bostic (phonetic sp.). Did you know that Bill Bostic…

items.title: James Moody interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998
items.q: And then when I heard Charlie Parker and Dizzy, I said that settles that.

ctx.x: I don’t know, they probably were because I saw some, but the C melody, the C melody, no that wasn’t — and then again, I really didn’t know either alto or tenor. Like I just wanted a saxophone you see? And then when I went to the theater and saw Lester Young and — no I didn’t see Lester Young but I mean I heard him on the records with Count Basie — well first of all, Jimmy Dorsey was my first inspiration, Jimmy Dorsey. So he played alto, so okay, well that could have been one of the reasons why I liked that. Then…

said no I like that better than the others. Then I heard Coleman Hawkins, and Prez. Now when I heard Hawk, he didn’t knock me out like Lester Young did. But when I got older, I realized that Hawk was playing the changes better than Lester Young. But Lester Young had that beat and that sound, you know [scats]. Oh I like that boy. And then when I heard Charlie Parker and Dizzy, I said that settles that. That’s it. Yep. So that’s how that happened. And then I was drafted in the Air Force. And they said, “Does anyone…
Did your band ever go to play for the white servicemen?
